newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Gujral says no missiles have been deployed.
newsitem.headline: India's Gujral says no missiles have been deployed.

text.p: Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral said on Wednesday reports about India's deployment of missiles on its border with Pakistan were a "deliberate misrepresentation".

"In technology we are going forward. It is no secret for me to say that we have acquired the missile technology, but it is wrong to say and a deliberate misrepresentation that we have deployed them," Gujral told reporters in this city in western India.
"I do hope this message will be taken in because we are keen to pursue peace in this region and we shall continue to do it," Gujral added.
He was speaking at an Indian Air Force base after inducting India's first Russian-made Sukhoi-30 fighter planes.

"Induction of the SU-30s would give the defence forces the necessary impetus to remain a force in the coming decades. The current geopolitical situation does not permit us to have a let-up in our defence preparedness," Gujral said.
On Monday, the Hindu newspaper said India had stored, but not deployed, medium-range ballistic missiles near its border with Pakistan.
The newspaper said the Prithvi missiles had been taken to Jullundur city in the northwestern state of Punjab but not deployed. It did not say where the missiles had been made.

The authoritative daily, quoting highly placed sources, said mere storage of the Indian-made weapons did not change the security balance between India and Pakistan, which have fought three wars since independence in 1947.

It said India's move could be compared to Pakistan's storing of Chinese-built M-11 missiles at Sargodha, which like Jullundur is near the border. Islambad denies it has obtained M-11 missiles from Beijing.

Last week, the Washington Post reported that India had moved fewer than a dozen Prithvi missiles, which can carry conventional but not nuclear warheads, to a prospective launch site near the Pakistani border.
Quoting U.S. officials, the newspaper said India's actions had raised fresh concerns that the two arch-rivals had entered a provocative phase in their arms race.
Some U.S. intelligence officials described the movement of the missiles as the first operational deployment of the Prithvi since its development began more than a decade ago.
But the Indian Defence Ministry said Prithvi missiles had not been deployed along the international border. Government officials declined to make any other comment.

India has tested the 250-km (150-mile) Prithvi missile, and a 150-km (90-mile) variant, and has vowed to press ahead with its missile programme despite opposition from the United States and other countries.
